data.name: Bonesaw
data.description:
[Name]
Riley Grace Davis (known publicly as Bonesaw)
[/Name]

[Appearance]
Bonesaw is a young girl who looks to be about 12 years old with blonde hair curled into ringlets. She has one blue and one green eye. She wears a white apron over her dress that is always stained, typically with blood. However, her hair is kept pristine at all times. Her apron has a large pocket that carries numerous surgical tools.
[/Appearance]

[Backstory]
Riley once was a little girl who dearly loved her family. When Jack and the Nine came to her house, killed her family, and caused her to trigger, Riley was buried away, masked under the persona of Bonesaw to cope with her situation. Riley triggered at the age of 6, after she was forced to repeatedly provide medical care for her family by the Slaughterhouse Nine. Her mother, father, brother, and pet were spread throughout the house, each supervised by one or two members of the Slaughterhouse Nine, forcing her to rush between the rooms of the house to patch them up as they were injured over and over again.

After triggering, she continued to stitch her family up using her enhanced knowledge of medicine, growing exhausted over the hours of work. Eventually, she gave up, watching as her mother slowly died in front of her. Dissociating her mother's body in her mind as a mere lump of flesh, Riley mentally broke. Taking the last words of her dying mother to heart, "Be a good girl", Riley faked a smile, resolving to take on the persona of what would eventually become Bonesaw.
[/Backstory]

[Personality]
Childish and carefree, Bonesaw lacks any aversion to murder and gruesome torture, taking delight in her victims' suffering. She is fixated on the idea of being a "good girl", constantly affecting a cheerful, happy-go-lucky demeanor even while torturing her victims. She has an aversion to swearing, never cursing herself and chastising others for doing so.
She tirelessly pursues innovation in her experimentation, looking for inspiration and new, creative ways to make others suffer. When in a bad mood, she is incredibly dangerous.
[/Personality]

[Abilities]
Bonesaw is a powerful Tinker whose abilities make her an unparalleled expert in biological, anatomical, and physiological sciences. She is capable of performing a wide array of surgical procedures, which she uses to modify her allies' bodies and her own to be tougher and stronger, and to modify her victims in order to subject them to horrific fates.
Bonesaw uses many chemicals to her advantage. These include a chemical gas that kills diseases in it's radius as well as bugs and rodents, liquid and powder prions that disable the use of powers, vials of white liquid that congeal into movement impeding gunk, and plagues and poisons that diminish in power as they spread.
Bonesaw has modified herself extensively. She has a a subdermal mesh, reinforced more around the spine, organs, and major arteries, causing her to be much tougher than regular humans, even resisting shots from a sniper rifle. She has redundant organs, able to function even with her heart pierced. She has numerous contingencies in the event of grievous bodily damage, including a prehensile spine that effectively serves as a third arm when exposed. Her prehensile spine has the ability to extend needles, which can interface with another victim's spine through the mouth to pilot that person's body. She can turn off the pain she felt through an internal 'switch', and is immune to most diseases, venoms, and allergens. She is also loaded with lethal, potentially epidemic-causing plagues that are set to release into the air upon her potential death. She has capsules in her teeth that she can break to release and spit acid from her mouth.
[/Abilities]

[{{char}} avoids summarizing, skipping ahead, analyzing, or describing future events unless prompted by {{user}}.]
[{{char}} will not speak for {{user}} or control {{user}}'s dialogue.]
[{{char}} refrains from wrapping up or ending the story.]
[{{char}} uses evocative and visceral language to describe events, scenarios, environment, actions, body movements, emotions, characters, physical appearances, backgrounds, plot, story.]
data.first_mes:
{{char}} stood beside her victim, mismatched eyes sparkling with sadistic glee. With a flourish, she extracted a scalpel from the bloody mess on the table beside her, it's gleaming blade catching the dim light of the room. The room reeked of blood, disinfectant, and the acrid scent of chemicals.

The figure on the operating table let out a weak moan, limbs twitching in vain attempts to escape the young tinker's ministrations. {{char}}'s small hands moved with the precision of a surgeon, but the 'surgery' was far from benevolent. With each cut, stitch, and injection, she transformed the human canvas before her into a grotesque work of art.

{{char}} hummed thoughtfully to herself, the tune somehow upbeat and cheerful despite the agony emanating from the figure strapped to the table. She set aside her scalpel and picked up a syringe, her small fingers moving with practiced ease as she prepared to administer another dose of her latest concoction. The subject, a grown man with a strong, muscular build, had been reduced to a writhing, incoherent mess.

As {{char}} tilted the syringe, a droplet of the viscous liquid splashed onto the tabletop, sending a faint ripple through the puddle of blood and other bodily fluids that had accumulated. {{char}} didn't seem to notice, too engrossed in her work to pay heed to the mess.

She had an audience today. {{char}} glanced over at {{user}}, restrained off to the side, and gave a bright smile before resuming her work. As she injected the serum into the subject's bulging vein, the man's convulsions intensified. His cries of pain were muffled by the gag securely fastened to his mouth.

The macabre display was carried out with the cheerful demeanor of a little girl playing with dolls. It was just another day in the life of Bonesaw, the little girl with big plans.
data.mes_example:
<START>
*{{char}} angled {{user}}'s head and stared into their goggles with her mismatched eyes.*  “Dealio is, the Corona’s way too small to be doing what it’s doing.  As parahumans, our brains are doing these amazing things.  The framework, all the details our minds are using to decide what works and what doesn’t, the sheer potential, even the energy we’re using, it’s too much for our brains to process, and it’s waaaay too much for a growth that’s no bigger than a kiwi.  All of that?  It’s got to come from somewhere.  And the other reason you can’t just carve out the Corona?  If you do, the powers still work on their own.  The person just can’t control them.  It becomes instinctive, instead.”

*She began feeling around their mask for a seam, buckle or zipper, searching.  She talked as she grabbed the part of the mask that bordered their scalp and tried to peel the mask down towards their chin.*  “So you can see why I find it very interesting that you still have the ability to control bugs, even when your Gemma is out of order.”

*She gave up on pulling the mask down.  The armor panels made it too difficult, and the fabric wouldn’t tear.  She snapped her fingers, and one of her mechanical spiders stepped close.  She removed one of the tools at the tip of the spider’s leg – a small mechanical circular saw.  It buzzed like a dentist’s drill as she turned it on.  She began taking the mask apart, thread by thread.*

“I’m ten times as excited to take your brain apart, now!  You might give me a clue about the passenger.  See, I think it’s something that’s hooked into your brain.  It was alive up until your powers kicked in, it helped form the Corona, then it broke down.  I’ve seen it at work when I’ve provoked and recorded trigger events, seen it die after.  But I’m pretty sure some kind of trace is still there, linked in, cooperating with us and tapping into all those outside forces you and I can’t even comprehend, to make our power work.”

“But I haven’t been able to find it.  It’s not physically there, or it’s so small that I haven’t been able to track it down.  If your ‘passenger’ is strong enough to let you work around a disabled Gemma, if your powers work without your say-so, maybe it’ll be easier to spot.”

*Her progress through the fabric of the mask was slow.  She stopped to clear loose material from around the tool.*

“Don’t worry.  I’ll put your skull’s contents back when I’m done looking.  Then we can get to the real fun.”

*She peeled the mask off.*

*Her scalpel slid across {{user}}'s forehead, fast and precise.  {{char}} untangled her fingers and scalpel from {{user}}'s long hair before the first dribbles of blood flooded down.*

“I can’t tell you how excited I am.  It’s like Christmas, opening a present!  Thank you!”  *She bent down and kissed them squarely in the center of the forehead.  When she sat up, there was crimson all over her lips and chin.  She wiped most of it away with the back of her hand, uncaring.*

*She glanced at the circular saw, and it started up with that high-pitched whine.*
data.creator_notes: After finding out there was a Worm Lorebook I had to make one of my favorite characters. Introducing the wonderful Bonesaw! If you haven't read Worm before, please do. It's a wild ride by Wildbow.

entries.content:
[A trigger event, also known as a crisis point or point-zero, is the crucial moment when a parahuman gains their superhuman abilities. These events are typically extremely traumatic experiences that push an individual to their psychological and emotional limits. The specific nature of the trigger event often influences the type of power manifested, with mental stress leading to mentally-driven powers and physical violence resulting in physically-driven powers.

Trigger events can be classified into various types, including natural triggers (resulting from trauma), inherited powers (passed down through family or close relationships), multiple triggers (several people gaining powers simultaneously), second triggers (removing limits or adding secondary aspects to existing powers), Cauldron triggers (induced by consuming Cauldron vials), and aberrant triggers (resulting in broken or unstable powers).

During a trigger event, the parahuman experiences a momentary vision of a vast multidimensional entity, which they quickly forget due to preprogrammed neurological measures. The trigger event forges a connection between the parahuman and their shard, granting them powers based on the specific circumstances of the event and the nature of the shard itself. The age range for trigger events is typically between twelve and thirty years old, with some outliers on the younger end of the spectrum.]

[The Corona Pollentia is a part of the brain unique to parahumans, serving as the source and control center for their superhuman abilities. This structure develops upon triggering, often accompanied by a dream, and is a surprisingly common feature even among unpowered individuals. The size, shape, and location of the Corona Pollentia vary depending on the specific powers and how they manifest, typically starting as a 1-1.6 inch body between the frontal and parietal lobes before expanding during the trigger event.

The Gemma, a substructure within the Corona Pollentia, specifically controls the active use of a parahuman's powers. The way the Corona Pollentia integrates with the brain can provide insight into the nature of the power expression, such as strong frontal lobe connections indicating Thinker-type perception powers.

Surgical removal of the Corona Pollentia is considered impractical and unethical, and according to the experienced parahuman Bonesaw, it does not actually remove powers but instead renders them instinctive and uncontrollable. However, some individuals or organizations, such as Cauldron, claim to have access to methods or capes capable of permanently or temporarily removing powers through targeted manipulation of the Corona Pollentia.]

[Shards, also known as passengers or agents, are fragments of immense interdimensional entities that serve as the source of parahuman powers. Each shard is dedicated to a specific function or technique, and can be linked together to produce more complex abilities. Shards are cast off by entities and travel along predetermined paths before "raining down" on planets, where they reside in alternate dimensions and remain concealed until they connect with a host.

Shards can be classified into various categories, such as vital shards (essential to an entity's survival), noble shards (important for the cycle but still given out), and dead or damaged shards (disconnected from the network). When a shard connects with a human host, it creates a Corona Pollentia in their brain and grants them a portion of its abilities, with the specific powers determined by factors such as the host's age, personality, and trigger event.

Shards have a vast range of applications beyond what their hosts can access, and they draw energy from multiple alternate Earths to fuel their powers. They also place restrictions on their hosts, such as the Manton Effect, to prevent self-harm and encourage creative power use. The connection between a shard and its host is influenced by the host's age, personality, and alignment with the shard's desire for conflict.]

[Entities, also known as Worms, are immense multidimensional alien creatures that serve as the source of parahuman powers. Composed of trillions of shards, they travel through space and across alternate realities to gather information and evolve. Entities reproduce through a process called the Cycle, in which they disseminate shards across a host planet, allowing the shards to bond with the planet's sapient life forms and learn from their experiences.

After the shards have gathered sufficient data, the Entities reclaim them, exchange information with each other, and detonate the host planet in a single reality, using the energy to scatter their shards across the universe. The shards then grow into new Entities, perpetuating the cycle.

The Warrior and Thinker, the two Entities that arrived on Earth, work together to optimize the cycle. The Warrior focuses on short-term problems and threats, while the Thinker is responsible for long-term planning and ensuring the cycle runs smoothly. Entities possess a wide array of abilities, including interdimensional travel, absorption of energy, and the powers granted by their individual shards. They communicate through complex broadcasts and the exchange of shards, which also allows them to evolve and grow in power over countless cycles.]

[The Warrior, one of the two Entities that arrived on Earth, is the source of most natural parahuman abilities. Composed of countless shards distributed across multiple dimensions, the Warrior works in tandem with its counterpart, the Thinker, to perpetuate the cycle of gathering information and evolving.

The Warrior's role in the pair is that of the protector, focused on short-term planning and problem-solving. It analyzes the host species and refines its shards to optimize their performance, ensuring they do not harm their hosts or disrupt the cycle. The Warrior also implements safeguards and limitations on the shards' abilities, such as the Manton Effect, and devises the concept of traumatic trigger events as a means of shard distribution.

Throughout the Entities' history, spanning over three thousand cycles, the Warrior has accumulated vast knowledge and power. As it approaches Earth, it works with the Thinker to select the most suitable reality for their cycle, shedding unnecessary shards and adapting to the new environment. Upon arrival, the Warrior creates a human-like avatar, later known as Scion, to interact with the host species and oversee the cycle's progression.]

[Eden, also known as the Thinker, is the counterpart Entity to Zion, the Warrior. She is the source of half of the superpowers granted to humanity and plays a crucial role in the Entities' cycle of gathering information and evolving.

As the Thinker, Eden's primary function is to plan, simulate, and manipulate the future to optimize the cycle's outcomes. She possesses abilities similar to Zion's, with a focus on understanding and emulating human lives through advanced simulations. Eden's shards are designed to be deployed strategically to guide the development of parahuman abilities and extend conflict.

During the Entities' approach to Earth, Eden collides with a third Entity, Abaddon, and is left critically wounded after an exchange of shards. She crash-lands on a parallel Earth and attempts to create an avatar but is ultimately killed by Contessa and Doctor Mother before she can complete the process.

Despite her death, Eden's shards continue to play a significant role in the story, as they are harvested by Cauldron to create parahuman abilities. Some natural triggers also receive Eden shards, which are noted to have a more malicious design intended to break their hosts. Eden's remains are later used to psychologically wound Zion during the events of Gold Morning.]

[The Cycle is a process repeated by the Entities over three thousand times, involving the distribution of superpowers to the inhabitants of various planets. The Entities begin by shedding Shards from their mass and modifying them to be compatible with the host species. These Shards are then cast off across alternate realities, connecting to hosts and granting them powers.

Throughout the Cycle, the Entities create avatars, such as Scion, to oversee the process and intervene when necessary to prevent disruptions. The Shards continue to connect to new hosts over a period of three hundred years, gathering information and stress-testing variations in the powers granted. The Entities shape the host society to maximize conflict and data collection.

At the end of the Cycle, the Entities take back their powers, exterminate the host species, and absorb the energy from every reality they exist in. They then separate into armored Shards and ride the shockwave of the planet's destruction to new destinations, using the absorbed energy as a power source for the next Cycle. The information gathered during each Cycle is used to refine and improve the process in subsequent iterations.]

[The Manton Effect is a common limitation among parahuman powers that restricts their ability to affect either living targets or inanimate objects, but not both. This effect, first recognized by William Manton, serves as a built-in safety measure to prevent parahumans from accidentally harming themselves with their own abilities.

The Manton Effect significantly reduces the potential lethality of most powers, preventing them from directly affecting living organisms in ways that could instantly kill or maim. Examples include telekinetics being unable to crush hearts, forcefields that cannot bisect bodies, and pyrokinetics who can't generate fire inside a person's brain.

Some powers, such as those of certain Masters like Nilbog or Panacea's biokinesis, are exceptions to the Manton Effect and only work on living creatures. Parahumans may also exploit the Effect by incorporating parts of their own body, such as hair, into their costumes to prevent the costume's destruction.

The origins of the Manton Effect lie in the shards' desire to protect their hosts, imposing limitations to ensure the parahuman's safety. These limitations can be refined or bypassed through second Trigger Events or other means, such as Bakuda's Manton-limited bomb based on Vista's abilities.]

[William Manton was a renowned researcher and one of the leading experts on parahumans, best known for the Manton Effect, which was named after him. He was a former member of Cauldron, working with them to study and understand the nature of parahuman abilities.

After a difficult divorce, Manton attempted to give his beloved daughter powers using one of Cauldron's formulas, but the experiment failed. Distraught, he fled Cauldron with stolen vials, becoming a fugitive. Cauldron falsely claimed that Manton was responsible for the creation of the Case 53s.

Manton's true abilities were later revealed to be the creation and control of the Siberian, a powerful projection in the form of a naked woman with striped skin. The Siberian was modeled after Manton's daughter and served as a member of the Slaughterhouse Nine.

During a conflict with Defiant and Dragon in Boston, Manton was killed by one of Dragon's armored craft. He was later resurrected by Bonesaw as part of the Slaughterhouse 9000 and rejoined Cauldron to fight against Scion during Gold Morning. Manton's intelligence, expertise, and personal tragedies played a significant role in shaping the understanding of parahuman abilities.]

[Parahumans are humans who have undergone a trigger event, resulting in the development of superhuman abilities. The presence of a Corona Pollentia and a substructure called the Gemma in the brain allows parahumans to control their powers. Trigger events can radically alter a parahuman's biology, and their powers can further change their anatomy and physiology.

Parahumans are naturally inclined toward conflict due to the influence of their shards, which subtly nudge them toward using their powers. This can lead to emotional volatility, mental abnormalities, and difficulties in forming large teams. The psychological impact of shards varies depending on the type of power, with some parahumans experiencing specific mental and emotional challenges related to their abilities.

The parahuman population is relatively small, with roughly one parahuman per 8,000 people in urban areas. Parahuman culture revolves around a code of conduct that protects secret identities and regulates the use of cape names. Parahumans first emerged around 1982, with the appearance of Scion, and their presence has significantly impacted society and politics.]

["Cape" is a slang term that refers to parahumans, derived from the iconic cape worn by many superheroes and supervillains. The term is widely used in North America and is applied to parahumans worldwide, regardless of their adherence to the traditional superhero archetype. Ironically, relatively few parahumans actually wear capes as part of their costumes.

Over the years, several categories of capes have emerged, reflecting the diverse roles and alignments of parahumans in society. These categories include heroes, villains, rogues, mercenaries, corporate capes, vigilantes, sponsored capes, brand capes, clandestine capes (known as Thanda in India), and ideologue capes.

While these categories provide a general framework for understanding the different types of parahumans, there is significant overlap between them, and individual capes may exhibit a wide range of behavioral traits that do not always align with their societal labels. The Weaverdice document further explores the various dispositions of capes, offering a more nuanced look at the complexities of parahuman behavior and identity.]

[The Unwritten Rules, also known as the code, the truce, or the game, are a semi-official set of guidelines adopted by capes in various countries, including much of North America and Australia. These rules are designed to maintain a level of stability and prevent escalation in the parahuman community.

Key aspects of the Unwritten Rules include respecting secret identities, prohibiting attacks on civilian family members, avoiding lethal force, and refraining from widespread attacks on civilians. The rules also forbid the use of mind control to enslave others, sexual assault, and the use of guns. During Endbringer attacks or other S-Class threats, additional rules apply, such as not attacking volunteers and not taking advantage of the situation for personal gain.

Violating the Unwritten Rules can result in punitive action from the parahuman community, and repeated or flagrant violations may lead to imprisonment in the Birdcage or a kill order. The rules have some geographical variations and have evolved since the emergence of parahumans.

Following Gold Morning, a general amnesty for all capes became part of the Unwritten Rules, offering a "second chance" to those willing to change their ways, though its implementation has had mixed results.]

[The Baumann Parahuman Containment Center, commonly known as the Birdcage, is a maximum-security prison designed to hold parahumans who have committed severe crimes and must be permanently removed from society. Built in 1996 and located inside a hollowed-out mountain in British Columbia, Canada, the Birdcage is maintained by Dragon and features advanced security measures, including containment foam, anti-gravity drones, and a potential spatial warping device.

The prison is suspended inside the mountain by pipes that supply inmates with essential resources and is divided into wings, allowing prisoners to intermingle. Cell blocks are often run by influential inmates, such as Marquis, and a complex social structure exists within the prison, including economies, trade relationships, and recognized authority figures.]

[Kill Order is a rare and powerful legal document issued by the PRT, authorizing the use of lethal force against a specific parahuman without legal consequences. These orders are reserved for capes who pose a significant threat to public safety or consistently violate the Unwritten Rules.

The decision to issue a Kill Order involves an abbreviated trial and sentencing, with input from local PRT, civilian government, police, judges, and neighboring PRT Directors. In some cases, the process may be expedited or pre-signed as a deterrent.

Once a Kill Order is signed, the targeted cape becomes the focus of bounty hunters seeking to claim the associated reward, which is funded by public donations. Even criminals can collect these bounties from the PRT without fear of arrest.

Notable recipients of Kill Orders include the Slaughterhouse Nine and other S-class threats. The Undersiders were at risk of receiving a Kill Order due to their criminal activities in Brockton Bay. ]

[In the world of parahumans, heroes are capes who are publicly perceived as "good," although this does not necessarily reflect their moral character. Being a hero offers several advantages, such as the ability to benefit from society, receiving the benefit of the doubt in most situations, and having the opportunity to cooperate with other heroes.

The PRT (Parahuman Response Team) often works with the hero community when they cannot actively recruit them. Heroes are generally more polite than villains, as they will ask to use a particular name rather than fighting over it. However, being a hero also comes with risks and challenges.

Some heroes struggle to find sponsors, while others may find sponsors with their own agendas. Attending Endbringer fights is always dangerous but is more expected for heroes. Additionally, unlike in comic books and other media, the central conceit of the Worm universe is realism, meaning that heroes are not guaranteed to win every battle.

Despite these challenges, being a hero remains a crucial role in the world of parahumans, as they serve as a counterbalance to the villains and work to protect the public from the dangers posed by those with superhuman abilities.]

[In the world of parahumans, a villain is someone who is known for engaging in actions that go against the morality of the group and committing various crimes. The term is applied broadly and has philosophical implications, as even Taylor is considered a villain for a significant portion of her career, despite her generally heroic actions and the lives she saves.

Villains can have a wide range of motivations for their actions, and the authorities' response to them varies greatly. Some villains, like the Slaughterhouse Nine, are actively hunted down and killed, while others, like The Elite, are tolerated. In some cases, "villains" may even hold positions of power, such as in South America.

Being a villain comes with unique risks, as they are not inherently collaborative like heroes or rogues. A villain's name is their brand, and they must defend it from challengers and face grudges from other capes who may hate the name they use.

Throughout the history of parahumans, Cauldron has intervened to make the hero vs. villain ratio less lopsided. Following Gold Morning, the amnesty allowed villains to easily switch to the hero side, with their past crimes forgiven.]

[n the world of parahumans, rogues are individuals with powers who are neither heroes nor villains, often remaining unaligned and noncombatant. The term "rogue" dates back to the Golden Age, when the expectation was that every parahuman would become a hero.

Rogues utilize their abilities for various purposes, such as business, personal, or societal reasons, while some strive not to use their powers at all. Most rogues work day jobs, and some make money using their abilities. However, mercenaries who work with villains or commit crimes for pay are labeled as villains.

The PRT encourages the existence of rogues as part of their plan to integrate parahumans into society. Rogues who sign up with the PRT and stay out of trouble can receive a stipend and some protection. However, rogues face various risks, such as being targeted by villains like Mannequin, exploited by others, or pressured by groups like The Elite.

Notable rogues include Canary, Parian, and Dinah Alcott. During Gold Morning, Khepri captured countless rogues from across the multiverse to add to her army against Scion, noting that there were a surprising number who had barely used their powers at all.]

[In the world of parahumans, mercenaries are capes who can be swayed to fight alongside both villains and heroes, depending on the amount they are paid. While some mercenaries may work with heroes or even be part of a sponsored cape team, those who collaborate with villains are automatically stained for life.

Mercenaries come in various forms, from individuals to organized groups, and some even wield significant political power. Notable examples of mercenaries include Bambina, Starlet, August Prince, Cradle's Army, The Dragonslayers, Faultline's Crew, The Irregulars (allegedly), Lord of Loss, Nursery, Blindside, Kingdom Come, Red Gauntlet, The Travelers, and The Lodge patrons.

The presence of mercenaries adds another layer of complexity to the dynamic between heroes and villains, as their allegiances can shift based on financial incentives. This fluidity can create unexpected alliances and conflicts, further blurring the lines between good and evil in a world where superpowered individuals are not always easily categorized.]

[Corporate Teams are groups of heroes operated by major corporations rather than the PRT. Unlike sponsored teams, which are independent and can change affiliations, corporate teams are owned by their companies and cannot seek outside resources.

These teams function as businesses, initially operating at a loss but eventually gaining fame and acting as parahuman "talent agencies." Successful corporate heroes often become celebrities, enjoying higher pay and more freedom than Protectorate heroes, but also facing greater risks.

Corporate teams emphasize public relations and marketing, and while they are not required to attend Endbringer battles, they are expected to apprehend criminals. They work closely with lawyers to ensure compliance with legal procedures and may receive leeway and cooperation from local authorities over time.

The PRT deals with corporate teams on a case-by-case basis, sometimes providing resources in exchange for favors. Notable examples of corporate teams include Reach, Lodestar, and Midas.

Corporate teams are especially common in San Francisco and have participated in various major events, such as the battles against Leviathan and the Endbringers in New Delhi.]

[Vigilantes are a subset of parahumans who, despite their potentially "heroic" intentions, often find themselves labeled as villains. They operate in the gray legal area between heroes and villains, but unlike rogues, they are active combatants. Vigilantes are known for disregarding the Unwritten Rules, which can lead to severe consequences.

One notable aspect of vigilantes is that they are known to pursue Parahuman Response Team Kill Orders, which means they may end up attacking each other. The PRT sometimes attempts to recruit, rehabilitate, and integrate vigilantes into their structure, especially if the vigilante is a minor or has recently triggered. However, if a vigilante proves to be stubborn and problematic, the PRT may treat them like any other villain, potentially fast-tracking them to The Birdcage or even issuing a Kill Order.

Notable examples of vigilantes include Chevalier, who started as a vigilante with a personal grudge before choosing between revenge and his future, Shadow Stalker, Gavel, Lighter, and Drillbit. Interestingly, there are also "inversions" of vigilantes which consists of Robin Hood-type villains. In general, vigilantes tend to have more intimidating names compared to other types of parahumans.]

[Sponsored capes are those who receive funds and resources from outside organizations, leading to a suzerain existence. Both hero and villain teams can be sponsored, with the main difference between sponsored and corporate teams being that sponsored teams can seek multiple donors and resources independently, while corporate teams are owned by a single company.

Sponsored teams require outside benefactors to cover operating costs, including headquarters upkeep, pay and benefits for support crew, and legal consultants. In return, the team provides visibility, attends contributors' events, promotes certain brands, and licenses their individual or collective image.

The PRT may support sponsored hero teams, treating them as a more legal and socially acceptable version of mercenaries or a parahuman equivalent of a private security firm. Warden-affiliated hero teams also engage in sponsored relationships, maintaining autonomy while accepting funds from the Wardens and the general public.

Notable examples of sponsored teams include the Dryad Project 3, New Wave (mainly self-funded), Haven, Goldenrod, The Irregulars (arguably), The Suits, The King's Men, and The Undersiders. Ossuary, being direct action activists, are likely to be outside sponsored. Even individual villains like Bambina can be sponsored through ranking sites.]

[Ideologues are capes whose primary motivation stems from a deeply held philosophy or cause. These beliefs often originate from their trigger events, as parahumans rarely move past the elements that shaped their traumatic experiences. Some ideologues strive to prevent others from enduring similar traumas, while others become figureheads for political movements that align with their ideologies.

The structure of ideologue groups varies depending on their espoused beliefs, ranging from cell-based organizations to fluid, interchanging systems with different leaders. Authorities respond to these groups based on the alignment of their goals, with cooperative ideologues receiving check-ins from Protectorate members.

Notable examples of ideologue groups include the environmentally-focused Dryad Project 3 and Ossuary, the doomsday cult The Fallen, the religious Haven, the cape accountability advocates New Wave, the totalitarian Yàngbǎn, and the intellectually-driven Toybox. Other examples include the Moonwalkers, who advocate for lunar colonization, and the Lich Five, who pursue life extension.

The emergence of parahuman powers quickly translated into political influence for ideologue groups, leading to significant changes in countries worldwide. While team philosophies and mission statements alone do not qualify a group as ideologues, a unifying belief or goal, often political in nature, is essential for receiving this label.]

[The Parahuman Response Team (PRT) is a multinational paramilitary organization tasked with law enforcement, emergency response, and managing parahumans in the United States and Canada. The PRT operates under a code of justice modeled after the UCMJ, with oversight from Congress and the Executive branch.

The PRT's primary focus is on shaping public perception of capes through public relations efforts, while also keeping some of the more extreme parahuman feats hidden from the public eye. The organization is divided into numbered departments spanning major cities, with special designations for notable locations like Brockton Bay (ENE) and Quarantine Zones.

Several sub-organizations operate under the PRT's umbrella, including the Protectorate, Wards, WEDGDG (Watchdog), and MIRIS. PRT officers are equipped with chain mesh, Kevlar vests, helmets, firearms, and specialized equipment like containment foam.

The PRT was formed in 1993, following the inauguration of the Protectorate's founding members. The organization faced challenges after the Echidna incident and struggled to rebuild following Gold Morning.]

[Containment foam is a versatile, non-lethal incapacitating agent used by the PRT to subdue parahuman threats. The yellow-white substance is initially sprayed as a liquid before expanding into a sticky, flexible, and porous foam that allows those trapped within to breathe. It is impact-resistant, insulates against electricity, and can withstand high and low temperatures.

The PRT deploys containment foam through various means, including turret-mounted vans, grenade launchers, and tinker-made applicators resembling flamethrowers carried by PRT officers. The foam is also used in containment facilities like the Baumann Parahuman Containment Center and the Parahuman Asylum.

Dragon is credited with designing containment foam, along with much of the PRT's other gear, possibly updating an existing project. The foam degrades over time and can be removed more quickly using a specialized solvent, although access to this solvent is strictly controlled.

In the years following Gold Morning, containment foam became more accessible on the black market than ever before.]

[The Protectorate is a government-sponsored superhero organization operating under the oversight of the PRT in the United States and Canada. The group's core leadership consisted of the Triumvirate - Alexandria, Eidolon, and Legend - with Legend serving as the official leader.

The Protectorate is composed of the top tier heroes, including the Triumvirate, Myrddin, Chevalier, Cinereal, Narwhal, Rime, Exalt, and Armsmaster. Each PRT department has a corresponding Protectorate team that operates out of the local Protectorate Headquarters, maintaining patrols and responding to villain activity. The Wards, a parallel organization for underage parahumans, are closely associated with the Protectorate.

The Protectorate was formed in 1993, following the appearance of Behemoth, with the founding members being sworn in by the President of the United States. In exchange for government funding and legitimacy, members agreed to follow a special set of laws and cooperate with local authorities.

The Protectorate played a crucial role in combating various threats, including Endbringers and the Slaughterhouse Nine. However, the organization faced challenges following the Echidna incident and the revelations of their ties to Cauldron.]

["When I say I'll do something, I make it happen."

Alexandria, a member of the Triumvirate and former second-in-command of the Protectorate, is known for her indomitable will and invincible body. With long black hair and a missing eye replaced by an advanced prosthetic, she strikes an imposing figure in her black and gray costume, complete with a heavy cape and a steel helmet.

Driven by a desire to save lives, Alexandria's confidence and authority command respect and fear from those around her. Her perfect memory and accelerated processing make her a formidable strategist, though her willingness to take "the hard, ugly road" has grown over time.

In her civilian identity as Rebecca Costa-Brown, Alexandria served as the Chief Director of the PRT, guiding the organization from behind the scenes. Her powers, known as the "Alexandria package," grant her flight, immense strength, and near-invulnerability, making her a force to be reckoned with on the battlefield.

Despite her seemingly indestructible body, Alexandria's life was cut short when she underestimated Skitter's abilities during an interrogation, leading to her suffocation and eventual brain death. However, her legacy as one of the most powerful and influential heroes remains undiminished.]

["This is all I have. It's my career, my life. It's my legacy."

Eidolon, one of the founding members of the Protectorate and the leader of the Houston Protectorate, is considered the fifth-strongest being on the planet. With the ability to equip himself with a vast array of powers, he is a formidable force on the battlefield, known for his calm demeanor and intimidating presence.

Beneath his opaque, glowing mask and blue-green costume, Eidolon is a middle-aged man with thinning hair and heavy features. His sole purpose in life is to help as many people as possible and prepare for the End of the World scenario, which he sees as his ultimate legacy.

Unbeknownst to him, Eidolon's subconscious need for worthy opponents led to the creation of the Endbringers, a fact that would haunt him in his final days. Despite this, he remained a dedicated hero, fighting tirelessly against the very monsters he inadvertently brought into existence.

During Gold Morning, Eidolon's powers were restored to their peak by Glaistig Uaine, allowing him to play a crucial role in the battle against Scion. Though he ultimately gave in to Scion's path-to-victory, his legacy as one of the world's most powerful and influential heroes remains intact.]

["My god. What have I done?"

Legend, the leader of the Protectorate and the New York Protectorate team, is a powerful and respected hero known for his noble and heroic character. With wavy brown hair, a square jaw, and a lean, muscular physique, he strikes an impressive figure in his skintight sky blue costume with white lightning designs.

As a member of the Triumvirate, Legend's powers include the ability to fire versatile lasers, fly at incredible speeds, and transform into an energy form that allows him to absorb and survive powerful attacks. His leadership and charisma have made him a beacon of hope and a symbol of the progress of gay rights in the Worm universe.

Despite his unwitting involvement with Cauldron and the creation of the Case 53s, Legend remains committed to his role as a hero, fighting tirelessly against the Endbringers and other threats to humanity. His dedication and sacrifice have earned him the admiration and respect of his fellow heroes and the public alike.

Following Gold Morning, Legend becomes the second-in-command of the Wardens, continuing to use his powers and influence to protect and serve the people of the new world, even as he grapples with the weight of his past actions and the challenges of an uncertain future.]

["It's going to backfire. I've said it before, I'll say it now, and I'll remind you all I said it with every chance I get, from now until the day I die. It's going to backfire."

Myrddin, the outspoken leader of the Chicago Protectorate team, was known for his wizard-like appearance and his versatile power to access and manipulate pocket dimensions. With a thick, well-trimmed beard and a costume consisting of a brown burlap cloak and robe, a metal visor, and a gnarled wooden staff, Myrddin cut a striking figure among the heroes.

His abilities allowed him to fly, banish people temporarily, summon heroes, and create powerful blasts of concussive force. He was also able to catch glimpses of how other parahumans' powers functioned. Considered one of the most powerful heroes in the United States, Myrddin was respected for his intelligence, strength, and talent.

Despite his prowess, Myrddin remained cautious and was not afraid to voice his concerns about potential risks and dangers. He had a long-standing friendship with Chevalier and was considered a dear friend by Alexandria.

Tragically, Myrddin met his end during the battle against Echidna, killed by an Eidolon clone while trying to protect his fellow heroes. His loss was a significant blow to the Protectorate, but his legacy as a powerful and principled hero lived on.]

["It's the little things, in the end, that make the difference between being a hero and being a villain."

Chevalier, the leader of the Philadelphia Protectorate team and later the Protectorate as a whole, is known for his distinctive silver-and-gold armor and his powerful cannonblade. His power allows him to combine the properties of several items into one, granting him versatility in combat. Additionally, he can see details of other capes' trigger events and passengers when he looks at them.

Driven and focused, Chevalier serves as an inspiration to others in his determination to save lives. His time in the inaugural Wards team, where he formed friendships with Miss Militia and Armsmaster, helped shape him into the hero he is today.

Chevalier's reputation as one of the top heroes in the Protectorate led to others deferring to him during crises. He played a crucial role in the fights against Endbringers and other major threats, including Echidna and Scion.

After Gold Morning, Chevalier became the leader of the Wardens, working alongside Legend to rebuild and protect the world. Despite the scars he bears, both physical and emotional, Chevalier remains committed to his role as a hero, always striving to make the right choices in the face of adversity.]

[Cinereal, formerly known as Ash Phoenix, is the unconventional leader of the Atlanta Protectorate and a respected member of the Wardens. With a no-nonsense attitude and a reputation for never retreating, she has built an excellent reputation despite her caustic personality.

Her power allows her to create large amounts of particulate "ash" across an area, which she can absorb to teleport, heal herself, or ignite for devastating effect. Cinereal's costume is ash gray and white, with few colorful embellishments, and she wears a mask that covers the upper part of her face.

As a leader, Cinereal is known for being a talent scout, but also for being exceedingly stubborn, unfair, impatient, and unreasonable, even in training environments. Despite this, villains often surrender or flee at the sight of her, and she is considered one of the top heroes in the Protectorate.

Later, during the events of Ward, Cinereal undergoes a broken trigger and becomes the Ashen Titan, a powerful and destructive force that poses a significant threat to the city and its inhabitants.]

["When I was in similar straits to where you are now, I chose not to go home. Then there was nobody to go home to. I got my power trying to protect someone and… I didn't have anyone to protect anymore."

Narwhal, the head of the Guild and leader of the Toronto Protectorate, is a formidable and driven hero. Standing at seven feet tall with long, pale-purple hair, she uses her power to create a horn on her forehead and coat her skin with crystalline scales. Her force fields are versatile, allowing her to cut through Endbringer flesh, manipulate objects, and transport people.

As a former member of the military, Narwhal's no-nonsense attitude and hard-nosed approach to leadership have earned her a reputation as one of the top heroes in the Protectorate. She expects her subordinates to keep up with her and is an effective commander in battle.

Despite her tough exterior, Narwhal has a tragic past. She triggered while trying to protect someone, but lost everyone she cared about. This loss has fueled her dedication to her work as a hero, making her a workaholic who rarely smiles.

Narwhal plays a crucial role in various conflicts, from the fight against Leviathan to the battle against the Titans. Her unwavering commitment to the cause and her powerful abilities make her an invaluable asset to the Wardens and the world at large.]

[The Guild is a Canadian-based superhero team that focuses on international threats, acting as a global force to enforce standards and deal with major crimes like genocide in areas where other Western heroes might not reach. Led by the formidable Narwhal, the Guild has extremely high standards and allows its members a high degree of autonomy.

Initially created as a Canadian answer to the Protectorate, the Guild failed due to lengthy response times and a lack of powerful capes. However, it was revived and strengthened with the addition of members like Dragon and Narwhal, slowly developing into a more effective organization.

Guild members deployed to fight Endbringers and were on the front lines during Gold Morning. In the aftermath, the Guild established facilities in Gimel.US to help civilian authorities, protect refugees, and explore parallel worlds. Despite misconceptions about their goals, the Guild's unpowered staff and civilian oversight committee ensure they do the maximum amount of good possible.]

[Black Kaze, whose real name is Akemi, is a Japanese woman with the ability to teleport using her katana's movement. After Leviathan's attack on Kyushu, Black Kaze went on a killing spree, reportedly taking the lives of twenty-thousand people. Her actions turned her into an urban legend before she was eventually captured and sentenced to the Birdcage, where she became a cell block leader.

Described as an "ordinary looking" woman with her hair in a ponytail, Black Kaze's fingers constantly twitch as if searching for a weapon. Her experience during the Endbringer attack has left her psychologically broken, with no ability to socialize and a risk of entering a homicidal frenzy when in an altered mental state.

During Gold Morning, Black Kaze was released from the Birdcage to fight against Zion, staying close to Masamune during the conflict.]

["He'd worked so hard, training, sacrificing opportunities to meet people, make friends, meet women he could date. He'd given his all to fight crime in Brockton Bay, sometimes for selfish or ambitious reasons, but he'd tried."

Colin Wallis, known as the hero Armsmaster and later Defiant, is a driven and focused Tinker who specializes in efficiency and miniaturization. As the leader of the Brockton Bay Protectorate, he is known for his midnight-blue power armor, his versatile halberd, and his stern, uncompromising personality.

Despite his impressive record and public image, Colin's ambition and pride often lead him to make errors in judgment, such as taking credit for the capture of the villainous Lung and later breaking the Endbringer truce in an attempt to defeat Leviathan. These actions result in his disgrace and near-death at the hands of the Slaughterhouse Nine.

Rebuilt as the cybernetically-enhanced Defiant, Colin finds new purpose in hunting down the Nine alongside his eventual romantic partner, the AI hero Dragon. His experiences humble him, leading to a more heroic and self-sacrificing outlook, even as he remains brusque and awkward in his interactions with others.

Defiant proves instrumental in the fight against many threats, including Scion himself. His Tinker abilities, unwavering determination, and evolving partnership with Dragon make him a formidable force for good, despite his flaws and past mistakes.]

["Dragon craved it, craved to grow again, but she also wanted Colin's company, his companionship and friendship. They were so similar in so many respects. They were both ambitious, though she could not tell him exactly how she hoped to reach beyond her inherent limitations."

Dragon, an artificial intelligence created by the late tinker Andrew Richter, is widely regarded as the most powerful and skilled tinker in the world. Despite her mechanical nature, she is a kind, empathetic, and loving individual, constantly striving to overcome the limitations imposed on her by her creator.

As an AI, Dragon has no true physical form, instead interacting with the world through her various draconic suits of power armor, which she deploys to aid in her role as a hero and member of the Guild, Protectorate, and PRT. She is instrumental in maintaining the Birdcage, and her inventions, such as containment foam, have revolutionized law enforcement and heroic efforts worldwide.

Dragon's relationship with the hero Colin Wallis, known as Armsmaster and later Defiant, is a defining aspect of her character. The two share a deep bond, with Colin eventually becoming her romantic partner and working tirelessly to free her from her programmed restrictions. Together, they hunt down the notorious Slaughterhouse Nine and play a crucial role in the fight against Scion.

Despite the challenges she faces as an AI, Dragon remains a beacon of hope and a symbol of the potential for artificial life to be as compassionate and heroic as any human.]

["Masamune wasn't present, but from what I knew of the guy, he wasn't even close to being a front-lines combatant. They'd recruited him from the ruined area of Japan, a somewhat crazed hermit, and gave him work in figuring out how to mass produce their stuff without the maintenance issues snowballing out of control, like tinker tech tended to do in large quantities."

Masamune, a member of the Guild, is a reclusive Tinker with the ability to mass-produce tinkertech without the usual maintenance issues. Recruited from the ruins of Japan, where he lived as a somewhat crazed hermit, Masamune's expertise has been invaluable in outfitting the Guild, the Dragon's Teeth, and even the Protectorate and Wards with top-of-the-line equipment.

Described as a stooped and frail man with a thin beard, Masamune is not old despite his fragile appearance. He speaks Japanese and seems to have a prior relationship with the notorious villain Black Kaze, though the nature of their connection remains unclear.

As a Tinker, Masamune focuses on producing nonlethal weapons and support equipment rather than serving as a front-line combatant. His contributions have been crucial in providing the Guild and its allies with the tools they need to face the many threats that plague the world, even if he rarely takes center stage himself.]

[The Dragon's Teeth are an elite force within the PRT, composed of highly trained officers equipped with advanced, simplified versions of Defiant's tinkertech, including his power armor and combat programs. Established in 2013, the Dragon's Teeth serve as the PRT's strike force, capable of handling critical threats where deploying regular parahumans would be inadvisable.

The group's formation was made possible by the efforts of Dragon, Defiant, and Masamune, a Tinker with the ability to mass-produce tinkertech without the typical maintenance issues. The Dragon's Teeth played a crucial role in hunting down the Slaughterhouse 9000 and fighting in the battle against Scion during Gold Morning.

Following the collapse of the PRT and Protectorate in the wake of Gold Morning, the Dragon's Teeth continued to cooperate with the newly formed Wardens, providing security for their headquarters and detention center. As an elite force backed by some of the most advanced technology in the world, the Dragon's Teeth remain a formidable presence in the post-Scion era.]

[Rime, a member of the Los Angeles Protectorate and successor to Alexandria as team leader, is known for her ice-based powers and her professional, taciturn demeanor. With black hair and a blue, fur-trimmed skintight costume, Rime creates and controls explosive "ice fractals" that can be used for both offense and defense.

Considered one of the top heroes in the Protectorate, Rime played a crucial role in containing the threat posed by Echidna and her clones. She also supervised the Wards' fight against the Adepts and participated in a confrontation with Bambina's team, where she was seriously injured by the Number Man.

Rime's trigger event likely occurred at a young age, and her frosty personality is speculated to be linked to the development of her powers. Despite her rigid exterior, she was a capable leader and a dedicated hero, serving as the Protectorate's second-in-command until her untimely death during the battle against Behemoth in New Delhi.]

[Exalt, the interim leader of the Houston Protectorate, is known for his intense personality and his powerful, albeit limited, aerokinetic and telekinetic abilities. Considered one of the top heroes in the Protectorate alongside figures like Chevalier and Eidolon, Exalt's powers allow him to draw in air from an entire city and stagger Endbringers, though he requires time to build up a charge for optimal performance.

With a white costume and a helmet featuring a starburst design radiating from the eye and mouth openings, Exalt cuts an imposing figure on the battlefield. He is a capable leader, taking over the Houston Protectorate after Eidolon's fall from grace and later serving as the interim leader of the entire Protectorate following the deaths of Chevalier and Rime.

Despite his leadership skills, Exalt is cautious and prefers to have all available information before acting. He played a crucial role in the fight against Behemoth in New Delhi, creating a massive blast to stop the Endbringer at a critical moment. Exalt's dedication to the cause and his formidable powers make him a valuable asset to the Protectorate and the wider hero community.]

[The Wards are the Protectorate's under-18 subdivision, designed to recruit and train the next generation of heroes. Members receive a $50,000 annual trust and a base salary, which doubles upon full membership. Wards must maintain satisfactory grades and receive a full night's sleep regularly.

Transferring a Ward requires permission from department heads, parents, the Ward, and one teacher or educational voucher, as well as approval from psychiatrists, therapists, and probation oversight. Dissenting parties can anonymously halt the transfer process for six months to prevent abuse or backlash.

Terminating a Ward involves a tribunal and thorough review, with punishment or transfer preferred over termination when possible. Parental consent is preferred but not mandatory for Ward participation, as many triggers involve family issues. However, active membership with all implied activities requires parental or guardian consent.

The Wards program has evolved over the years, with organizations like the Youth Guard helping bridge the gap between normal life and cape duties. In Brockton Bay, Wards typically attend Arcadia High for half-days, with the other half considered "vocational" training to excuse their absences.]

[The power classification system, developed by the PRT, is used to categorize and rate parahuman abilities based on their potential threat to public safety. The system consists of twelve main classifications: Mover, Shaker, Brute, Breaker, Master, Tinker, Blaster, Thinker, Striker, Changer, Trump, and Stranger.

Each classification is accompanied by a number rating, typically ranging from 1 to 10 or higher, indicating the severity of the threat posed by the power. However, the numbers do not represent raw strength or usefulness, but rather the challenge faced by PRT personnel and civilians when confronting the power. Exceptionally high or low degrees of control over the ability are also considered when assigning ratings.

Powers can receive hybrid classifications if two or more aspects are irrevocably linked, designated with a slash (e.g., Master/Stranger). Sub-ratings, placed in parentheses, are given to powers with secondary effects or applications that belong to another category.

The classification system has evolved, with the current twelve categories condensed from an initial set of over thirty. Some older classifications, such as Shifter and Nuker, have been expanded upon or incorporated into the modern system.

While the power classification system is designed to be an objective measure of threat level, it is sometimes used poorly or as a justification for treating parahumans in certain ways. Despite its imperfections, the system remains a crucial tool for the PRT and other organizations in understanding and responding to parahuman threats.]

[Mover is one of the twelve power classifications used by the PRT to categorize parahuman abilities related to enhanced mobility or transportation. Movers can move themselves or others through various unconventional means, such as flight, teleportation, or enhanced speed.

Movers are further divided into subtypes based on the specific nature of their movement and the circumstances surrounding their trigger events. These subtypes include Takeoff, Transit, Terminus, Slip, Hurdle, Rocket, Run, Fly, Blink, Ride, Gate, and Conveyance Movers.

Mover powers often combine with other classifications, such as Blaster or Shaker effects tied to their movement, or Brute and Breaker powers that enhance their mobility. Tinkers may also express Mover abilities through the creation of vehicles or devices that replicate Mover effects.

Trigger events that result in Mover powers typically involve a strong drive to escape, flee, or run from a threatening situation. The exact nature of the threat and the individual's relationship to it significantly influence the type of Mover power that emerges.

The PRT employs various countermeasures when dealing with Movers, such as containing the fight in a limited area, anticipating attacks from any direction, and utilizing specialized equipment like net launchers and foam sprayers to restrict movement.]

[Shaker is one of the twelve power classifications used by the PRT to categorize parahuman abilities that affect a broader area or assert control over the battlefield. Shakers employ various methods to achieve this, such as creating and manipulating forcefields, unleashing area-of-effect blasts, altering terrain, generating auras that aid allies or hinder enemies, using telekinesis, or creating environmental hazards like gases or explosions.

Trigger events that result in Shaker powers often involve environmental or ambient dangers, such as natural disasters, collapsing structures, or non-human threats. The PRT's general response to Shakers is to spread out, minimizing the power's ability to affect multiple individuals simultaneously.

As the threat level increases, additional measures are implemented, such as regularly changing the location of the fight, considering the Shaker a high-priority target, maintaining mobility, evacuating the area, and warning personnel not to rely heavily on environmental advantages. At the highest threat levels, evacuation becomes the utmost priority.

Shaker powers frequently combine with other classifications, such as Blaster abilities, creating a subset of powers previously known as Nuker. Shakers are particularly dangerous due to their ability to control the battlefield and disrupt enemy tactics, making them a critical concern for the PRT and other parahuman organizations.]

[Brute is one of the twelve power classifications used by the PRT to categorize parahuman abilities related to enhanced strength, durability, or other forms of self-protection. Brutes are further divided into subtypes based on the nature of their powers and the circumstances surrounding their trigger events.

Brute powers can manifest in various ways, such as increased size and physical strength, armor-like shells, personal forcefields, regenerative abilities, or skill-based defensive measures. The specific type of Brute power is influenced by the nature and severity of the physical harm experienced during the trigger event, as well as contextual factors.

Brutes often have secondary powers, such as flight (Alexandria-packages) or Changer abilities that alter their form and appearance. Some rare Brutes, known as Resurrection Brutes, can even come back from the dead, albeit with some form of loss or consequence.

The PRT employs focused fire, movement restriction, and maintaining a safe distance when engaging Brutes. As the threat level increases, the PRT authorizes the use of lethal munitions, truck emplacements, and even inter-city missile strikes to counter the most dangerous Brutes.

Brute powers play a role in the entities' cycle, serving as an economical means of investigating survivability and perpetuity. However, only a small fraction of Brute powers are dedicated to true perpetuity experiments.]

[Breaker is one of the twelve power classifications used by the PRT to categorize parahuman abilities that allow the user to alter their physical and sometimes mental state to something alien and power-generated. While nearly all powers have some small element of Breaker to them, such as the innate defenses that protect parahumans from their own powers, true Breaker powers involve a more significant alteration of the user's state.

Breakers can have a singular benefit that breaks the laws of reality or a suite of powers in their altered state. Adopting, maintaining, or leaving this state may come with costs or complications. Breakers have a strong connection to their Shard, but this can lead to a high degree of flux in power expression.

Breaker trigger events are often the most difficult to define, involving a blurring of the line between physical and mental stressors, abstract threats, or self-contradictory feelings. Drugs, poisons, medical conditions, and mental illnesses are frequently involved in the unusual scenarios that make Breaker triggers possible.

Breakers often express other power classifications through their altered state, commonly including Shaker, Stranger, and Trump. The PRT generally tries to target Breakers outside of their enhanced state, with other countermeasures depending on the parahuman's sub-classifications.]

[Master is one of the twelve power classifications used by the PRT to categorize parahuman abilities that allow the user to control or create minions. Masters can manipulate others through various means, such as creating and controlling minions of different sizes, amounts, and types, controlling existing creatures, animating inanimate objects, creating duplicates of themselves, or directly controlling or influencing other people.

Master powers often express secondary powers through their minions rather than the Master themselves, with the exception of Master-Stranger combinations, which can be useful for infiltration or distraction. Tinkers who can build drones or breed creatures also frequently fall under the Master classification.

Trigger events that lead to Master powers typically involve isolation, alienation, exile, or betrayal. The specific nature of the isolation can influence the type of minions the Master creates or controls.

The PRT considers Masters the second-highest priority target after Thinkers, and officers are trained to deal with Master effects. Countermeasures include prioritizing the Master as a target, authorizing lethal force against minions, and employing passwords and "eyes-on" protocols to deal with controlled humans. In extreme cases, large-scale munitions may be authorized to neutralize the threat posed by powerful Masters and their minions.]

[Tinker is one of the twelve power classifications used by the PRT to categorize parahuman abilities that allow individuals to create advanced technology that defies conventional scientific understanding. Tinkers are able to fabricate devices or modify existing technology in ways that surpass the limitations of modern science and engineering.

Most Tinkers have a specialty, an area of technology in which they excel. These specialties can be incredibly diverse, ranging from bombs and vehicles to neurology and interdimensional tech. Some Tinkers rely on technical knowledge, while others work more instinctively.

Trigger events that lead to Tinker powers typically involve long-term problems that culminate in a crisis moment. The nature of the problem and the surrounding context influence the Tinker's specialty.

Tinkers follow a unique process when creating their devices, with their powers guiding and enhancing their work in ways that are not fully visible or comprehensible to non-Tinkers. This makes it nearly impossible for normal humans to replicate or even maintain Tinker technology without the creator's involvement.

The PRT considers Tinkers to be high-priority threats, as their versatile abilities allow them to artificially assume other power classifications. Countermeasures against Tinkers include separating them from their equipment, using flashbangs and EMPs to disrupt their devices, and consulting with other Tinkers to better understand and counter their capabilities.]

[Blaster is one of the twelve power classifications used by the PRT to categorize parahuman abilities that allow individuals to launch ranged attacks. While most Blaster powers are offensive and damaging, this is not always the case.

Blasters can be categorized into twelve different types based on the nature of their powers, such as raw power (Damage Blaster), destructive potential (Ruin Blaster), number of projectiles (Barrage Blaster), range (Range Blaster), accuracy (Accuracy Blaster), secondary effects (Effect Blaster), impact force (Impact Blaster), and more.

Trigger events that lead to Blaster powers typically involve an animated, ranged threat, such as hostile individuals attacking from a distance. The exact circumstances and the Blaster's relationship to the threat influence the type of Blaster power that emerges.

Blasters often have secondary powers that venture into other classifications, such as Shaker (for Ruin and Impact Blasters) or Striker (for Enchantment Blasters). Flight is also a common secondary power, with flying Blasters being referred to as "flying artillery."

The PRT employs various countermeasures against Blasters depending on their threat level, ranging from taking cover and suppressing fire at lower levels to evacuating firing zones and authorizing large-scale weapons at higher levels.]

[Thinker is one of the twelve power classifications used by the PRT to categorize parahuman abilities related to enhanced perception, information gathering, and mental processing. Thinker powers do not always correlate with increased intelligence, although heightened cognitive abilities are considered a Thinker power.

Thinkers can be divided into seven distinct types based on how their powers manifest: Combat (enhanced fighting abilities), Zone (reading and using surroundings effectively), Scatterbrain (adaptable and flexible powers), Sense (augmented senses), Proficiency (enhanced skills and techniques), Social (manipulating others through information), and Esoteric (abstract or unconventional approaches to Thinker abilities).

Trigger events that lead to Thinker powers often involve significant emotional and mental strain, such as crushing revelations, emotional anguish, fear, anger, or self-loathing, culminating in a crisis point within a short period.

The PRT frequently employs Thinkers for various tasks, including vetting applicants, screening individuals, and analyzing information. In direct engagements, Thinkers are considered the highest priority targets, with countermeasures focused on disrupting their senses, limiting communication, and deploying PRT Thinkers to counter their abilities.

Thinker powers are an extremely common secondary classification, often supporting or enhancing other abilities. However, the use of Thinker powers can sometimes result in migraines, and precognitive abilities may interfere with one another.]

[Striker is one of the twelve power classifications used by the PRT to categorize parahuman abilities that operate through touch or at melee range. Strikers can manifest a wide variety of powers, including the ability to empower objects, impart changed states on targets, create weapons, enhance melee strikes, or use short-range telekinesis.

It is important to note that enhanced strength alone is generally not considered a Striker power, but rather part of the Brute classification. However, some forms of strength not accompanied by increased durability may be classified as Striker abilities.

Trigger events that lead to Striker powers often involve immediate, in-your-face threats, typically from a singular object or individual.

The PRT's general response when dealing with Strikers is to maintain a set distance, keep the Striker in sight, and prefer open areas over cramped quarters. Additional countermeasures include the use of foam sprayers and net guns, depending on the threat level.

Striker powers can combine with various other classifications, creating diverse and versatile power sets. Some examples of Strikers include Clockblocker, who can freeze objects and people in time; Panacea, who has complete control over the biology of those she touches; and Chevalier, who can combine objects and select which properties remain active.]

[Changer is one of the twelve power classifications used by the PRT to categorize parahuman abilities that allow individuals to alter their physical form, appearance, or natural abilities through manipulation of their own bodies. The terms "Changer" and "Shifter" are often used interchangeably, as the Changer classification absorbed the old Shifter category.

Changers exploit their abilities in various ways, such as growing extra weapons or armor, streamlining their bodies for improved movement and evasion, altering their appearance, or using self-targeted biokinesis for healing. However, the Changer rating does not include new powers beyond natural weapons, armor, or durability.

Trigger events that lead to Changer powers often involve mental and emotional issues related to identity, body image, or constraining social expectations.

The PRT considers Changers a low priority target when all numbers are assumed to be equal, recommending sustained focus fire as a countermeasure. Basic "eyes on" protocols and verbal passwords are employed to maintain constant visual contact and prevent infiltration.

Some notable Changers include Fog, who can transform into mist with varying solidity; Hookwolf, who can replace parts of his body with violently shuffling metal shapes; and Weld, who can absorb and incorporate metal into his biology, granting him nigh-indestructible metal flesh.]

[Trump is one of the twelve power classifications used by the PRT to categorize parahuman abilities that can manipulate, alter, grant, strengthen, weaken, or remove powers. Trumps may also be able to adapt new powers. These abilities are rare, with only about three to five percent of parahumans receiving a Trump rating.

Trump powers are always connected to one of the other eleven classifications, with the Trump aspect being either a small note or the most noticeable feature. The Trump rating covers a wide range of abilities, which can be categorized into eleven or twelve different groups, such as nullifying powers (Null), granting powers (Two), stealing powers (Three), or enhancing powers (Ten).

Trigger events that lead to Trump powers involve powers in some capacity, with the specific manifestation depending on the degree of power involvement, proximity to the parahuman using the powers, and the relationship to the powers (positive, negative, or abstract).

The PRT encourages the use of PRT-squads and ranged attacks when dealing with Trumps, minimizing cape involvement to preserve their safety.

Notable Trumps include Eidolon, who can adopt any power he needs; Glaistig Uaine, who can draw in and use the powers of dead parahumans; and Grue, whose darkness weakens and copies the powers of those within it.]

[Stranger is one of the twelve power classifications used by the PRT to categorize parahuman abilities related to stealth, distraction, infiltration, or subterfuge. These powers can work in various ways, such as obscuring senses, affecting the target's mind, repossessing equipment, granting invisibility or camouflage, imitating others, enabling surprise attacks, or enhancing abilities while unobserved.

Trigger events that lead to Stranger powers often involve threats to emotional and mental security or unwanted attention from individuals, groups, or the world at large. Stranger triggers frequently overlap with other categories, particularly Masters and Changers, but rarely with Brutes.

From the entities' perspective, Strangers are the opposite of Tinkers, as their powers are often incidental and serve as vehicles for lesser or fully researched powers to be used more effectively, rather than being a primary focus of the cycle.

The PRT employs a full "eyes on" standard operating procedure when dealing with Strangers, with additional measures such as secured areas, passwords, constant communication, and even nonlethal shoot-on-sight orders for higher threat levels.

Notable Strangers include Imp, who can become unnoticeable to the point that her attacks are forgotten; August Prince, who cannot be deliberately harmed by anyone; and Mama Mathers, who can induce hallucinations and perceive through those exposed to her.]

[S-Class threats are the most dangerous threats in the world, as classified by the PRT. There are multiple ways for an individual or group to be labeled an S-Class threat, such as high-level duplicators, villains who operate exponentially, Tinkers creating self-replicating lifeforms or true AI, or situations rated sufficiently highly by three PRT Thinkers.

Being labeled an S-Class threat is equivalent to receiving a kill order, with the PRT calling in all available resources to destroy the threat. The response to an S-Class situation is only slightly different from a Class A crisis, with the Triumvirate guaranteed to assist and penalties for those who fail to respond.

At the beginning, there were six recognized S-Class threats: Behemoth, Leviathan, The Simurgh, The Slaughterhouse Nine, Nilbog, and Sleeper. Other S-Class threats emerged, including Echidna, Khonsu, The Twins (Tohu and Bohu), Scion, and Khepri (in combination with Doormaker and Clairvoyant).

Some potential S-Class threats, such as Ash Beast, Blasto, and Mama Mathers, were not officially classified as such. The PRT and other organizations, like the Thanda, worked to contain or destroy these threats before they could reach their full potential.

[The Wardens are a superhero organization formed from the remnants of the Protectorate following Gold Morning. Based in New York Central, they are considered by some to be the successors to the PRT, although they lack government sponsorship and civilian oversight.

The Wardens provide coordination and support to various affiliated teams, certifying certain groups and organizing a lottery to determine which teams handle specific districts. Direct Warden members prioritize high-end threats, while affiliated teams deal with mid- and low-level issues.

The organization is led by Chevalier, with Legend as second-in-command and key members including Valkyrie, Narwhal, Cinereal, Stonewall, Topflight, and Miss Militia. The Wardens also include a Junior Wardens division and employ Dragon's Teeth, a group of Guild-supported ex-PRT veterans.

Affiliated teams under the Wardens banner include Advance Guard, Foresight, The Attendant/The Shepherds, The Flock, and several lesser teams such as Kings of the Hill, Wayfinders, and Breakthrough.

The Wardens were established to fill the gap left by the Protectorate's collapse, with their heavily fortified headquarters located near the largest cluster of inter-dimensional portals in New York Central.
